zone: Twin Lakes and Yellow Aster Butte
_areas_note: Two trailheads on one road serve this zone. Twin Lakes Road (FR 3065) leaves the Mount Baker Highway about twelve miles above Glacier; at roughly 4.5 miles it reaches the Tomyhoi Lake / Yellow Aster Butte trailhead at about 3,700 ft, and the last two miles climb to the Twin Lakes basin at 5,200 ft. Winchester Mountain, Mount Larrabee and American Border Peak are all approached from the road end at Twin Lakes by way of the Winchester and High Pass trails. Tomyhoi Peak is the odd one out on the same road: it is climbed from the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead at 4.5 miles, over the Gold Run Pass junction and up to the tarns, not from Twin Lakes. Goat Mountain has been REMOVED from this zone. It is not on Twin Lakes Road at all: its trail leaves Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32) about 2.3 miles up from the Mount Baker Highway, at roughly 2,550 ft in the Ruth Creek valley, a separate drainage several miles further east along the highway. Its camping is a different problem entirely (forested benches and a ridge crest with almost no water above the low switchbacks) and it should be researched with the Hannegan Pass Road peaks.

sites.name: Twin Lakes Road upper section and the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead pullouts
sites.capacity: A dozen or so vehicles in the trailhead lot, plus scattered pullouts along the road; it fills on summer weekends and there is nowhere to turn around if you keep going and change your mind
sites.water: Creeks cross the road in places but there is nothing reliable at the lot itself; carry water up from the valley or plan to filter higher
sites.permit: A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and the state parks pass is not accepted here. Fill in the free self-issue wilderness permit at the register where one is provided. Dispersed roadside camping on national forest land outside the wilderness boundary is generally allowed, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a pullout.
sites.notes: This entry is the road rather than a campsite, because on this approach the road is the variable that decides what the trip is. The first four and a half miles to the Tomyhoi Lake and Yellow Aster Butte trailhead are rough gravel that an ordinary car can manage with patience; the straight section below the switchbacks is the worst of it, with loose rock and deep potholes. The final two miles to Twin Lakes are narrow, unmaintained for passenger cars, short of pullouts, and genuinely want high clearance. Parties turned back at the lower lot are looking at an extra two miles and roughly 1,500 ft of road walking each way before the climb even starts, which turns a comfortable day on Winchester or a two-day Larrabee trip into something much longer, and is a good reason to plan on sleeping out. The road is snowbound well into the season most years and is often not drivable to the upper end until July. Call the ranger station before committing, and if you park low, camping in a pullout the night before is a common and reasonable way to save the morning.

sites.name: Twin Lakes basin road-end camp
sites.capacity: Roughly ten to fifteen informal sites spread around the two lakes; first come, first served, and competitive on any decent summer weekend
sites.water: The two lakes, right at camp. No treated water; filter or boil.
sites.permit: Recreation pass or the posted per-vehicle day-use fee for the trailhead. Free self-issue wilderness permit at the register for anyone continuing onto the trails. The lakes basin at the road end sits outside the wilderness and several sites have metal fire rings, but everything above and beyond is wilderness where fires are prohibited outright, and county or forest-wide burn bans routinely close the road-end rings as well. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve. Hang or canister your food.
sites.notes: This is the base for everything on the north side of the zone. An alpine cirque at 5,200 ft with the two lakes, subalpine trees and meadow, vault toilets at both lakes, picnic tables at many sites, and no drinking water. Because you can drive to it in a capable vehicle it is the only place in the zone where a heavy pack costs you nothing, so most parties on Winchester, Mount Larrabee and American Border Peak sleep here and start from the isthmus between the lakes. The Winchester Mountain trail and the High Pass trail both begin there. It does not melt out completely until July in most years, and late-season parties should expect a busy, social camp rather than a quiet one. Everything the lakes hold is heavily used; pick an established site rather than making a new one in the meadow.

sites.name: Winchester Mountain Lookout
sites.capacity: Two bunks inside and floor space for a couple more at a squeeze; twelve is the legal party limit but the building comfortably holds far fewer
sites.water: None at the summit. Carry everything up from Twin Lakes, or melt snow early in the season.
sites.permit: Free, no reservations, no fee, and no way to book it. Locked from November through May, reopening when conditions allow, and off limits as a shelter in winter beyond stepping inside with the shutters left as they are. Wilderness rules apply on the trail and at the summit: no fires at all, party size twelve, no toilet, so pack out everything including human waste.
sites.notes: A 1935 lookout on the 6,521 ft summit, kept standing by volunteers from a local hiking club rather than by the agency, and genuinely open for anyone to sleep in on a first-come basis. It is 1.7 miles and about 1,300 ft above the Twin Lakes trailhead, which makes it one of the easiest real summits in the range to reach and a fine advance camp for a light party heading on to Mount Larrabee, though it sits off the direct High Pass line and most climbers heading for American Border Peak carry on past the junction rather than up. Treat the building as borrowed. It survives on people sweeping it out, closing the shutters properly, packing out their rubbish and leaving it drier than they found it; a run of poor behaviour is exactly why the winter season was closed. Always carry a tent or bivy, because it may well be occupied when you arrive and there is only room for two on the bunks. There are patches of ground outside the building flat enough to sleep on. The trail crosses steep, exposed snow slopes that linger into July and sometimes August, and an ice axe is the right call before the traverse is bare.

sites.name: High Pass camp
sites.capacity: A couple of small tent spots on and just below the pass; two or three tents at most, and they are exposed
sites.water: Nothing running. Snow patches into midsummer are the only source, so most parties carry water from Twin Lakes or drop to the creek at the mine basin below.
sites.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. Mount Baker Wilderness rules: no fires, party size twelve, camp on durable ground, pack out all waste including human waste. The international boundary runs a little over a mile north of the pass; camp and climb south of it, and see the border note on the mine basin below.
sites.notes: High Pass is reached from the Twin Lakes isthmus by way of the Winchester junction, a traverse under an avalanche chute, then Low Pass and a short climb, roughly two and a half miles with a little over a thousand feet of gain. It is directly on the line for both of the big objectives here: the basin north of the pass leads to the south face of Mount Larrabee and its standard south ridge scramble, and the same ground continues around Larrabee's west slope towards American Border Peak. Camping at the pass buys you height and a very short morning, and costs you water and shelter, since it is a windy notch with almost nothing flat. The snow slopes between Twin Lakes and the pass are the crux of the approach for much of the season and can stay steep and firm into August. Parties who want to sleep dry and drink freely usually pass over the top and drop into the mine basin instead.

sites.name: Gargett Mine basin bivy
sites.capacity: Room for only a few bivy sacks at the old mine workings themselves; several tent sites on the gravel bars in the green basin a few hundred feet lower
sites.water: A creek runs through the basin by the old mine, and it is the last reliable water on the way to either summit; everything beyond is snowmelt or nothing
sites.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. No fires anywhere in the wilderness, party size twelve, pack out all waste including human waste. The old mine is an abandoned working, not a shelter; stay out of any adit. The international boundary is the other thing to have straight before you leave camp: American Border Peak's summit stands just south of it and its twin across the connecting col to the north is in another country, so on this climb the line is a route-finding constraint and not an abstraction. It is unmarked on the ground for most of its length here, there is no port of entry anywhere near, and there is no way to present yourself to either country's customs from the mountains, so crossing it, whether by carrying on along a summit ridge or dropping down the far side of a col, is an illegal entry rather than a technicality and can cost you at a staffed crossing later. Know where the line runs before you leave camp and stay south of it. This is patrolled country, so being asked for identification on the road or in the basin is routine; carry photo identification, and proof of status if you are not a citizen.
sites.notes: This is the base camp for American Border Peak and for the west side of Mount Larrabee, and it is what turns both from a punishing single push into a sane two-day trip. From High Pass a boot path drops north and west into the basin, reached in well under an hour from the pass and about two and a half hours from the Twin Lakes trailhead. The workings themselves sit on a bench with space for a handful of people lying down, and the friendlier option is to keep descending a few hundred feet to the green basin below, where gravel bars beside the creek take proper tents. From here the American Border Peak approach traverses Larrabee's west slope to a notch around 6,200 ft and on into the moraine bowl below the south saddle, which is the reason parties who try the peak in a day so often run out of daylight. Fill every bottle before you leave the creek. Snow lingers in the bowls above the basin all summer, and the ground is loose scree and gravel that will not hold a stake well.

sites.name: Yellow Aster Butte tarns (Yellow Aster Meadows)
sites.capacity: Perhaps eight to ten small sites among the tarns, all of them well used; expect company, and expect to take whichever pad is left rather than the one you wanted
sites.water: The tarns themselves. They are shallow, warm late in the season and shared with a great many campers, so filter and draw well away from where people wash.
sites.permit: This basin has its own rule and it is strictly enforced in spirit if not always in practice: no camping within one mile of the Yellow Aster Butte trail EXCEPT at the tarns. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, never on the heather. No fires anywhere on the trail. Pack out all human waste; do not bury it. Party size twelve, and food must be canistered, in a protective sack or hung well clear of the ground and trunk. Recreation pass at the trailhead, free self-issue wilderness permit at the register.
sites.notes: The standard camp for the southeast ridge of Tomyhoi Peak, and the reason Tomyhoi is a comfortable overnight rather than a very long day. From the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead at about 3,700 ft the trail climbs towards Gold Run Pass, forks left onto the meadows trail and reaches the scatter of tarns at roughly 5,580 ft in about four miles. From camp the route drops northwest over a hump to a col near 6,266 ft and follows the ridge over benches and a small glacier remnant to the false summit and the class 3 summit block. This is one of the most heavily impacted alpine basins in the district and the rules exist because the meadow was being destroyed; a single careless night on heather leaves a scar that lasts years. Mountain goats frequent the basin, are habituated, and will come to camp for the salt in urine, so pee on rock well away from the tents. Snow covers the basin into July and the tarns can still be part frozen at the start of the season.

sites.name: Tomyhoi Lake
sites.capacity: A handful of rough forested sites at the lake; quiet, and rarely full
sites.permit: No camping within one mile of Gold Run Pass, which rules out the whole upper part of the descent; the lake itself is far enough down to be legal. Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register, recreation pass on the vehicle, no fires, party size twelve, pack out waste.
sites.notes: Worth knowing about mostly so you do not plan a climb around it. Despite the name, Tomyhoi Lake is not the camp for Tomyhoi Peak: the trail from the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead climbs to Gold Run Pass and then loses roughly 1,500 ft over two miles down the far side to the lake at about 3,727 ft, while the peak's southeast ridge starts from the tarns high above. Camping here and climbing the peak means regaining everything you gave away. It is a good option for a party that wants a low, sheltered, uncrowded night in the trees when the meadows are snowed under or the tarns are full, and it is the natural bail if weather closes the high ground. The last stretch of trail down to the lake is brushy and easy to lose, and the north side of Gold Run Pass is steep, exposed and holds snow into late summer, so carry an axe and traction if you are dropping in early in the season.
